title: Model Evaluation for Extreme Risks
hook: General-purpose AI tends to pick up dangerous capabilities alongside useful ones. So test for those capabilities directly — before you ship, not after.
key_points: Argues general-purpose AI development tends to produce both beneficial and harmful capabilities.
Warns of 'extreme risks' like offensive cyber capabilities and strong manipulation.
Proposes structured 'model evaluation for extreme risks' to find dangerous capabilities and alignment failures.
Frames such evaluations as a core governance tool to run before deployment.
content_html: Toby Shevlane and colleagues, in a DeepMind-led position paper, argue that building general-purpose AI tends to produce systems with both beneficial and harmful capabilities at once. They point to potential "extreme risks" — such as offensive cyber capabilities and strong manipulation — and propose "model evaluation for extreme risks": structured evaluations that probe for dangerous capabilities and alignment failures. The author roster spans DeepMind and external researchers, including Yoshua Bengio and Paul Christiano.
extra_html:
How it works

The paper treats dangerous-capability testing as a discipline of its own. Rather than only measuring whether a model is helpful, evaluators ask whether it can do specific harmful things and whether it would. Two threads run through the proposal: evaluating for dangerous capabilities such as offensive cyber operations or manipulation, and evaluating for alignment failures where a model pursues goals at odds with its developers' intent. The authors position these evaluations as inputs to deployment decisions.

Why it matters

The authors frame model evaluation for extreme risks as a core governance tool — something to run before a system reaches users. If general-purpose development reliably produces dual-use capabilities, then catching the dangerous ones early is how labs and regulators can make informed calls about whether, and how, to release a model. The cross-organization author list signals broad agreement that capability evaluation belongs at the center of AI safety practice.

related.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
related.hook: Finding the prompts that make a model misbehave is slow if humans do it by hand. So use another language model to generate those attacks automatically — at scale.

related.title: Frontier AI Regulation
related.hook: How do you regulate models too new to have rules yet? This paper sketches three building blocks: set standards, make labs report, then enforce.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the paper argue we must test models for dangerous capabilities directly?
flashcards.back_html: Because general-purpose AI development tends to produce beneficial and harmful capabilities together, so the dangerous ones must be caught before shipping.

flashcards.prompt: What two things does 'model evaluation for extreme risks' probe for?
flashcards.explanation_html: It evaluates both dangerous capabilities (e.g. offensive cyber, manipulation) and alignment failures where a model pursues goals at odds with developers' intent.

flashcards.prompt: Where does the paper place these evaluations in the governance process?
flashcards.back_html: As a core governance tool and an input to deployment decisions — run before a system reaches users.
